newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Burma conducting joint opium survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Burma conducting joint opium survey.

text.p: The United States and Burma -- a country that Washington says does not cooperate in the war against drugs -- are conducting a joint survey of opium production in Burma, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.
They said narcotics experts from the two countries were scheduled to begin a joint opium yield survey on March 9. It was not possible to establish whether the six-day survey had begun as scheduled.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the survey would enable experts to measure production of opium in Burma, one of the largest producers in the world.

U.S. officials say about 60 percent of the heroin reaching the United States comes from Southeast Asia, most of it from Burma. The "Golden Triangle" drug producing area is on the borders of Burma, Thailand and Laos.
Officials said previous joint surveys had taken place in 1993 and 1995.
Despite that, the United States last month again "decertified" Burma in an annual report for failing to cooperate in the struggle against drug trafficking.

Burns said the joint survey would not involve any aid to the Burmese government and "does nothing to take away our very great concern about the gross and negligent treatment of narcotics by the military dictators who rule Burma".

"The only thing that's going to help Burma get off the decertification list is if they stop growing opium and having the government subsidise it and look the other way when the drug lords try to export that opium and other drugs from Burma," he told a news briefing.

The United States has frigid relations with Burma because of its human rights practices and failure to respect the results of a 1990 election won by opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi, winner of the Nobel peace prize.
